body: Swedish licence plates are long and white, with a blue EU strip. Taxis have distinctive yellow plates.
The Swedish language uses the unique letters Å, Ä, and Ö. While Finland shares Ä and Ö, its words are longer with double vowels, distinguishing it from Swedish.
Sweden uses only white road lines. On smaller roads, the outer lines are short and dashed, which helps distinguish them from the longer dashed lines in Norway.
Swedish highways have outer road lines with a unique pattern of small sections, appearing solid from afar. This is different from the solid lines in Finland and Norway.
Swedish bollards are black-and-white with a grey or orange reflector. They come in various shapes including wedge-shaped, round, or thin and curved.
Swedish snow poles are orange with a tall white reflector positioned slightly above the middle. A second, thinner reflector can sometimes be seen above the main one.
Swedish utility poles are typically wooden and often feature a small black metal cap on top, a common feature in Nordic countries.
Street lamps on wooden poles in Sweden are mounted slightly below the top with a double bolting. This helps distinguish them from Finnish lamps, which are mounted at the very top.
Wooden electricity markers with a blue and white stripe at the top are unique to Sweden.
Swedish pedestrian signs have four stripes. A version with a female silhouette is a unique feature of Sweden.
Swedish directional signs are usually blue with a thin white arrow. Smaller roads may have yellow signs with a red border.
Swedish warning signs have a yellow background with a red border. This is different from Finnish signs, which have an additional thin yellow border.
Sweden is one of the only countries in Europe to use chevrons with yellow arrows on a blue background.
Blue signs with a large white 'M' indicate meeting points on smaller roads. The Swedish 'M' is distinct from the Norwegian version as its middle point does not extend to the bottom.
Swedish signposts often have striped markings. While blue and white is common elsewhere, red and yellow stripes are a strong indicator for Sweden.
A lot of road infrastructure in Sweden, like road work signs and road blocks, is painted red and yellow.
Common Swedish street suffixes are -vägen and -gatan, often appearing as separate words. These are different from the attached suffixes in Norway or the Danish 'vej' and 'gade'.
Swedish houses are often wooden and painted a distinct dark red, a colour common in Nordic countries. Urban architecture is modern, while suburban areas feature freestanding homes.
Sweden's landscape is varied, featuring boreal forests, farmlands, and many lakes. The north and west are mountainous, while the south and east are flatter.
A traditional Swedish wooden fence made of stacked diagonal and vertical trunks is a very common sight.
Volvo is the most common car brand in Sweden, accounting for nearly 30% of all passenger cars.
The Swedish church flag, a red cross on a yellow background with a crown, is often seen near churches.
Much of Sweden's Generation 3 coverage features a white car with a long antenna. This car is also common in Iceland and Finland, but rare in Norway and Denmark.
Generation 4 coverage in Sweden can feature a red, white, or blue car. The presence of a red or white car is a strong clue for Sweden, as only the blue car is found in other Nordic countries.
Sweden features Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, which has a lower viewpoint and a large circular blur. This camera is common across Northern Europe.
Broad-leafed trees (other than birch) are a good indicator for the southern half of Sweden.
Ferns are typically found in southern and central Sweden.
Mountains with no trees at the top are a strong clue for northwestern Sweden.
Thin, weak-looking boreal trees on sandy soil are characteristic of the far north of Sweden.
Beech forests with barren, leafy ground are a strong indicator for the far south of Sweden.
Rock walls are most common in the south, especially along the coast and on the islands of Öland and Gotland.
Exposed, rounded rocks are a common sight on the west coast. In contrast, rocks around Stockholm are sharper and often covered in thick moss.
Skåne, in the south, has the most open agricultural landscape in Sweden, with sparse patches of trees and diverse crops.
The region around Lake Mälaren is characterized by flat, medium-sized fields with forests beyond and small 'islands' of trees within the fields.
The farmlands of Västergötland and Östergötland are flat and open, similar to the Mälaren region but with more wind turbines and more distant forests.
Sweden's west coast, especially Halland, features flat fields with small, round, forested hills in the distance and a very lush look.
Flat, small to medium-sized agricultural fields in the northern half of the country suggest a location near the coast between Umeå and Luleå.
Jämtland County features large, uncultivated grass fields situated on wide, steep hills, a landscape uncommon elsewhere in Sweden.
The High Coast (Höga Kusten) is recognizable by its forested, rocky mountains surrounding agricultural valleys of varying shapes.
In Södermanland, agricultural fields often run through small valleys with forests on the hillsides.
White sand next to roads is a good clue for the island of Gotland, especially in the north.
Red dirt roads mainly appear in Dalarna, but also in Kalmar county, the border between inland Norrbotten and Västerbotten, and rarely between lakes Vänern and Vättern.
Deep grey dirt roads with low green grassy vegetation are common in northern Jämtland during summer (Gen 4) and fall (Gen 3).
Öland is a very flat island with a barren south half, lush north half, and many small rock walls.
Long, neat rows of moderately thin birches are common along the north coast in urban areas.
Grey metal roofs become increasingly common northwards on residential buildings, though barns and sheds can have metal roofs further south.
Skåne houses often have white stone or red brick walls with coloured wooden triangles under the roof; similar houses appear elsewhere in southern Sweden.
Half-timbered houses mainly appear in southern Skåne, northern Skåne, southern Halland, and occasionally Visby.
Many single-family houses in Skåne are built with red brick, typically looking older than bricks elsewhere.
Southern Sweden, especially Skåne and Blekinge, have corrugated metal roofs with moss, usually on steep barns.
Grey diamond-tiled roofs are typical in Skåne, Blekinge, Öland, and sometimes Gotland.
Houses on Sweden's west coast, especially between Gothenburg and Norway, are often lighter colored, mainly white and light yellow.
Northern west coast's coastal towns commonly have dense rows of very small red sheds.
Central Dalarna has unique wooden architecture with red timbered houses, log portals, and distinct hӓrbren designs.
Hälsingland features large red farmhouses with many windows, 2-3 floors, and barns with numerous windows.
Northern coast has agricultural sheds either octagonal or rectangular with outward leaning red-painted log walls.
Gotland houses commonly made of limestone with a dirty white facade and churches with grey or white walls and small divided windows.
Uneven stone brick walls are typical on Öland houses and rock walls, less so on Gotland.
Each Swedish administrative region has unique bus stop signs.
Many regions feature distinct bus shelters, which may complement or replace bus stop signs.
Sweden has national (9-99) and regional (100-404) numbered roads; numbers generally increase northeast.
Red crosses mark snowmobile trails across northern Sweden.
Western Dalarna roads often have red color, with thin pine forests, indicating the region.
Green snow poles are occasionally found around Umeå.
Wedge-shaped bollards similar to Germany’s occur mainly in southern Sweden.
Cylindrical bollards with horizontal black bands are common near west coast, Värmland, and southern Dalarna.
Flat or cylindrical bollards with black reflectors dominate major roads in northern Sweden.
Small white bollards with blue or red stripes near the top appear in rural Skåne.
Railway crossing signs have a yellow sticker with a 5-digit ID, where the first digit indicates region, increasing northeast.
Place name endings are often region-specific, helpful for location guesses, but exceptions exist.
Sámi bilingual signs occur inland in northern Sweden.
Meänkieli language, related to Finnish, occurs near the Finnish border, often on river names and trilingual signs.
Gotland's Generation 3 coverage has a slight green blur, similar to blurs seen in Estonia.
A white Google car with a blue stripe is mostly found along the Swedish west coast and in Skåne.
Swedish landline phone numbers start with region-specific area codes, varying by region; mobile numbers start with 07.
The E10 road between Kiruna and the Norwegian border has small birches, pines, snow-covered mountains, and a major lake to the north.
Northern road 99 features grey sandy ground, brown-green moss, ditches, and a dense mixed forest of birches, pines, and spruces.
Road to Ritsem has a large lake to the south and dramatic mountains, is small, paved without road lines, with summer and early spring coverage.
Road between Kittelfjäll and Norwegian border is narrow, paved without road lines, going through mountains, covered in summer Gen 2.
Most Swedish mountain roads are below the treeline; one stretch on the Jämtland-Västerbotten border has no visible trees, making it unique.
Sweden’s highest altitude public road is a dirt road over a treeless mountain plateau in cloudy Generation 4 summer conditions.
Kiruna’s two mining mountains, with staircase-like layers, are notable town landmarks also visible from the E10 road.
Gällivare is near a naturally treeless mountain with smooth slopes and a low tree line.
Flat agricultural fields with a forested hill range to the west indicate being east of Omberg in western Östergötland.
Mistletoe is mostly found near Lake Mälaren, especially in Västerås.
Visingsö island in Lake Vättern is recognizable by agricultural fields with the lake on both sides and forested hills on shores.
Most Swedish large orchards are near Kivik on Skåne’s east coast, also northeast of Kristianstad, around Båstad, and the southern east coast of Lake Vättern.
Northern west coast of Öland features a small coastal road with a rocky beach and low bushy vegetation.
Fårö island near Gotland has small dry stony fields with tiny green bushes, more extreme near the north coast.
Southern tip of Gotland has a west coast road with grassy fields and a grassy hill ridge to the east.
Old factory towns called Walloon mills near Uppsala have rows of identical residential houses made of brightly coloured stone or red wood.
Blue or green slag stone buildings are rare and found mainly in the mining region of Bergslagen.
Öland has numerous small grey and sometimes red wooden windmills, more than any other Swedish region.
Red brick chimneys with crown-like tops or rectangular holes are common near Lake Siljan and often painted white.
Visby is the only preserved Hanseatic town in Sweden, known for cobblestone streets, small bright stone houses, abundant roses, and the old Hanseatic wall.
Old Stockholm features warm-colored old stone buildings and narrow cobblestone alleys.
Cities and towns have their own local bus stop signs, distinct from regional signs.
Neon yellow school bus stop signs are frequent in Linköping, Norrköping, and Jönköping.
Kungsbacka municipality uses bus stops with three blue stripes; these stripes appear throughout Halland.
Trams are mostly in Gothenburg, then Norrköping and Stockholm, and rarely in Lund.
Black bus shelters with a square ridge on the roof back are in Västerås and Umeå.
Stockholm street signs have two rows separated by a black line, usually without black borders; similar signs occur in central Gävle.
Gothenburg uses unique blue street signs with almost always two lines; other cities have blue signs with different designs.
Malmö features somewhat old white street signs with black corners.
Ystad has signs similar to Malmö but with yellow backgrounds.
Blue street signs like Gothenburg’s but with one line are found in Vellinge municipality.
Plain yellow street signs occur in Falköping; yellow signs are rare elsewhere and always bright.
Blue street signs with thin black outlines are typical in Köping.
Street names ending in ‘gattu’ or ‘gatu’ are found in central Dalarna, near Lake Siljan.
Elfdalian language is exclusive to around Älvdalen, visible on street signs with endings like ‘-ween’ or ‘-weg’.
Three yellow stripes appear on signposts and lamps in Karlstad and on traffic lights in Stockholm.
Small yellow tree felling signs are seen on poles and lamp posts in Stockholm suburbs, often showing the city's phone code.
Sundsvall is known as Drakstaden (Dragon City), with dragon statues and signs in the center.
The E4 road between Umeå and Finnish border has wide ditches/barriers, flat landscape, and forests with thin birches and pines.
Mountainous areas near the Norwegian border on E12 have orange snow poles with two wide reflectors.
Near the Norwegian border on road 95, yellow snow poles with two white reflectors are common, with autumn and snowy generation 4 coverage.
Road E10 near the Norwegian border shows a mix of orange and yellow snow poles.
Road 95 west of Arjeplog features Generation 4 thawing snow coverage in a mountainous landscape.
Umeå city has Generation 4 spring coverage with thawing dirty snow piles along roads.
E45 road between Orsa and Älvros features brown-red wet pavement and thin pine and birch forests.
Holmön island has Generation 3 coverage with a white car and long antenna showing a distinctive visual glitch.
Foskrosvägen on Jämtland-Dalarna border has red dirt roads and visible water smudges on cameras.
